anchor.title: Reichsparteitag of the NSDAP in Nuremberg, SA troops march past Adolf Hitler, Sept. 1935
anchor.creator: Charles Russell (donor) / National Archives and Records Administration (NARA)
anchor.citation: Russell, Charles. "Reichsparteitag of the NSDAP in Nuremberg, SA Troops March Past Adolf Hitler, Sept. 1935." September 1935. National Archives and Records Administration (NAID 558779), via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Reichsparteitag_of_the_NSDAP_in_Nuremberg,_SA_troops_march_past_Adolf_Hitler,_Sept._1935.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph showing a massive parade of SA troops marching past Adolf Hitler at the Nazi Party Rally in Nuremberg, Germany, September 1935.
anchor.caption: This photograph from September 1935 shows the Nazi Party's annual rally in Nuremberg, Germany, where thousands of SA troops march in formation past Adolf Hitler. The scale of this event — with tens of thousands of uniformed men assembled in perfect order — captures the power and organization of the fascist movement that Hitler had built in Germany. By 1935, Hitler had been in power for two years and had turned Germany into a one-party totalitarian state. These massive rallies were carefully designed as public displays of Nazi power, using spectacle, symbolism, and the sheer size of crowds to inspire loyalty and intimidate opponents. This image represents the kind of totalitarian political theater that Mussolini pioneered in Italy and Hitler adopted and expanded in Germany — using mass mobilization to make the state appear all-powerful and inevitable.

anchor.title: Buchenwald Slave Laborers Liberation (April 16, 1945)
anchor.creator: Private H. Miller / U.S. Army Signal Corps
anchor.citation: Miller, H. "Buchenwald Slave Laborers Liberation." 16 Apr. 1945. U.S. Army Signal Corps / National Archives and Records Administration, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Buchenwald_Slave_Laborers_Liberation.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white U.S. Army photograph taken on April 16, 1945, showing emaciated Jewish slave laborers in the barracks at Buchenwald concentration camp near Weimar, Germany, five days after liberation.
anchor.caption: This photograph, taken on April 16, 1945, shows survivors in the barracks at Buchenwald concentration camp near Weimar, Germany, five days after American forces liberated the camp on April 11. The men — Jewish prisoners who had been used as forced labor — are visibly emaciated from years of systematic starvation. Nobel Peace Prize laureate Elie Wiesel is visible in the second row. Buchenwald was one of the largest concentration camps in Nazi Germany. When American soldiers of the 80th Division entered the camp, they found thousands of survivors in conditions of extreme deprivation, as well as evidence of mass murder. General Eisenhower ordered extensive documentation of what was found in the camps, understanding that the world needed to see the proof of Nazi atrocities with their own eyes. Images like this one became central to understanding the Holocaust — the Nazi regime's systematic murder of six million Jews and millions of others.

anchor.title: USS Shaw Exploding During the Japanese Raid on Pearl Harbor, T.H. (80-G-16871)
anchor.creator: Unknown U.S. Navy photographer / U.S. Navy
anchor.citation: Unknown U.S. Navy photographer. "USS Shaw Exploding During the Japanese Raid on Pearl Harbor, T.H." 7 Dec. 1941. U.S. Navy / National Archives and Records Administration, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:USS_SHAW_exploding_Pearl_Harbor_Nara_80-G-16871_2.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white U.S. Navy photograph showing the USS Shaw destroyer exploding in a massive fireball in Drydock No. 2 during the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, December 7, 1941.
anchor.caption: This photograph captures one of the most dramatic moments of the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941 — the explosion of the USS Shaw in Drydock No. 2. The massive fireball and smoke column illustrate the sudden, devastating power of the surprise Japanese attack that killed more than 2,400 Americans and plunged the United States into World War II. The attack was delivered without a formal declaration of war, while Japanese diplomats were still meeting with American officials in Washington. President Roosevelt called December 7th 'a date which will live in infamy' when he asked Congress for a declaration of war the next day. The destruction at Pearl Harbor ended years of American isolationism almost overnight and unified the country behind the war effort. Images like this one made the abstract threat of war suddenly and terrifyingly real for millions of Americans who saw them in newspapers and newsreels.

anchor.title: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima (February 23, 1945)
anchor.creator: Joe Rosenthal / Associated Press (remade from NARA File 520748)
anchor.citation: Rosenthal, Joe. "Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima." 23 Feb. 1945. Associated Press / National Archives and Records Administration, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Raising_the_Flag_on_Iwo_Jima,_by_Joe_Rosenthal.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph by Joe Rosenthal showing six U.S. Marines raising the American flag atop Mount Suribachi on Iwo Jima, February 23, 1945.
anchor.caption: This iconic photograph by AP photographer Joe Rosenthal captures six U.S. Marines raising the American flag atop Mount Suribachi on Iwo Jima, Japan, on February 23, 1945. The Battle of Iwo Jima was one of the fiercest and most costly battles of the Pacific campaign — the 36-day battle to capture this small volcanic island resulted in very heavy casualties on both sides. The island was strategically critical because of its location and its airfields, which could be used for both emergency landings by American bombers and for staging attacks on Japan. The flag-raising on Suribachi, the island's highest peak, symbolized a major military achievement in the brutal Pacific island-hopping campaign. The photograph quickly became one of the most famous images of World War II and was used to inspire war bond purchases and recruitment. It later became the model for the U.S. Marine Corps War Memorial in Arlington, Virginia, permanently enshrining this moment of sacrifice and determination in American military memory.

anchor.title: Tuskegee Airmen, 332nd Fighter Group, Ramitelli, Italy (March 1945)
anchor.creator: Toni Frissell / Library of Congress, Toni Frissell Collection
anchor.citation: Frissell, Toni. "Tuskegee Airmen, 332nd Fighter Group, Ramitelli, Italy." Mar. 1945. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, Toni Frissell Collection, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Tuskegee_airmen_2_original.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph by Toni Frissell showing several Tuskegee Airmen of the 332nd Fighter Group posing in front of an aircraft at Ramitelli, Italy, March 1945.
anchor.caption: This photograph taken at Ramitelli, Italy, in March 1945 shows Tuskegee Airmen of the 332nd Fighter Group — the first African American military aviators in the U.S. armed forces. Trained at Tuskegee Army Air Field in Alabama during World War II, they flew combat escort missions protecting Allied bombers on missions over Europe. The Tuskegee Airmen served in a racially segregated military in which many doubted Black Americans' abilities as combat aviators. Their exceptional service record — including an outstanding record protecting the bombers they escorted — helped disprove racist stereotypes and build the argument for military desegregation. The 'Double V' campaign — fighting for victory abroad and victory over racism at home — captured the spirit of Black Americans who served their country even while fighting discrimination. The Tuskegee Airmen's legacy contributed directly to President Truman's decision to desegregate the U.S. military with Executive Order 9981 in 1948.

anchor.title: Operating a Hand Drill at Vultee-Nashville, Woman is Working on a ‘Vengeance’ Dive Bomber, Tennessee (February 1943)
anchor.creator: Alfred T. Palmer / U.S. Office of War Information (OWI) / Farm Security Administration
anchor.citation: Palmer, Alfred T. "Operating a Hand Drill at Vultee-Nashville, Woman Working on a Vengeance Dive Bomber, Tennessee." Feb. 1943. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, FSA/OWI Color Photographs Collection (LC-USW36-295), www.loc.gov/item/2017878540/.
anchor.alt: Color OWI photograph by Alfred T. Palmer showing a woman in work clothes and a head scarf operating a hand drill on the fuselage of a Vultee A-31 Vengeance dive bomber at the Vultee Aircraft factory in Nashville, Tennessee, February 1943.
anchor.caption: This color photograph from February 1943 shows a woman operating a hand drill on a Vultee A-31 Vengeance dive bomber at the Vultee Aircraft factory in Nashville, Tennessee. Taken by Alfred T. Palmer for the U.S. Office of War Information, this image captures one of the most significant social transformations of World War II: the massive entry of American women into the industrial workforce. When millions of men left for military service after Pearl Harbor, the defense industry faced a critical labor shortage. Women were recruited — and in many cases eagerly answered the call — to work in aircraft factories, shipyards, and munitions plants. By 1944, nearly 20 million American women were employed, many for the first time in industrial jobs. The cultural icon of 'Rosie the Riveter' captured this transformation and became one of the defining images of the war era. Although most women were pressured to leave industrial jobs when the men returned after the war, the experience permanently expanded ideas about women's capabilities and contributed to the long-term growth of the women's rights movement.

anchor.title: "White" & "Black" Work Side by Side — North American Aviation Co. Plant (c. 1942)
anchor.creator: Unknown / U.S. Army Signal Corps / Office of War Information
anchor.citation: Unknown / U.S. Army Signal Corps. "'White' & 'Black' Work Side by Side — North American Aviation Co. Plant." c. 1942. National Archives and Records Administration (NAID 195477), via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:%22White%22_%26_%22Black%22_work_side_by_side_-_North_American_Aviation_Co._Plant_-_NARA_-_195477.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white U.S. Army Signal Corps photograph captioned 'White and Black work side by side' showing White and Black workers on the same production line at the North American Aviation Co. plant in Inglewood, California, circa 1942.
anchor.caption: This circa 1942 photograph of the North American Aviation Company plant in Inglewood, California, shows White and Black workers employed together on the same production line — a scene that was notable enough that the photographer or the Army Signal Corps felt it warranted documentation and the caption 'White and Black work side by side.' Before World War II, most defense industry employers discriminated against African Americans, refusing to hire them for skilled or semi-skilled industrial jobs. Executive Order 8802, signed by President Roosevelt on June 25, 1941, banned such discrimination in defense industries and government and created the Fair Employment Practices Committee. As a result, hundreds of thousands of African Americans moved north and west to take defense industry jobs, improving their economic circumstances while continuing to serve in a racially segregated military. The Double V campaign — fighting for victory abroad and victory over racism at home — captured the dual struggle of Black Americans during World War II. This photograph documents both the limited progress made through Executive Order 8802 and the ongoing struggle for full racial equality.

anchor.title: Photograph of Members of the Mochida Family Awaiting Evacuation Bus, Hayward, California (May 8, 1942)
anchor.creator: Dorothea Lange / War Relocation Authority / National Archives and Records Administration
anchor.citation: Lange, Dorothea. "Photograph of Members of the Mochida Family Awaiting Evacuation Bus, Hayward, California." 8 May 1942. U.S. Department of the Interior, War Relocation Authority / National Archives and Records Administration (NAID 537505), via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Photograph_of_Members_of_the_Mochida_Family_Awaiting_Evacuation_-_NARA_-_537505.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph by Dorothea Lange showing members of the Mochida family — including parents and several children wearing identification tags — seated on benches awaiting the evacuation bus in Hayward, California, May 8, 1942.
anchor.caption: This photograph, taken by Dorothea Lange on May 8, 1942, shows members of the Mochida family waiting to board the evacuation bus that will take them to a War Relocation Authority internment camp. The family patriarch had operated a nursery in Hayward, California, growing snapdragons and sweet peas. Each family member wears an identification tag. This image documents one of the most controversial civil liberties violations in American history: the forced relocation and internment of approximately 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry — about two-thirds of them U.S. citizens — following President Roosevelt's Executive Order 9066, signed on February 19, 1942. The internment was driven by racial prejudice and wartime hysteria, not evidence of any actual disloyalty. The Supreme Court upheld the policy in Korematsu v. United States, 323 U.S. 214 (1944). In 1988, Congress formally apologized and paid reparations to surviving internees. Photographs by Dorothea Lange served as crucial documentary evidence of the human cost of the internment — evidence so powerful that the U.S. Army actually confiscated some of Lange's images during the war.

anchor.title: Mushroom Cloud above Nagasaki after Atomic Bombing, August 9, 1945
anchor.creator: Charles Levy / U.S. Army Air Forces / National Archives and Records Administration
anchor.citation: Levy, Charles. "Mushroom Cloud above Nagasaki after Atomic Bombing." 9 Aug. 1945. U.S. Army Air Forces / National Archives and Records Administration, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Nagasakibomb.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white U.S. Army Air Forces photograph showing the enormous mushroom cloud rising above Nagasaki, Japan, after the detonation of the 'Fat Man' atomic bomb on August 9, 1945.
anchor.caption: This U.S. Army Air Forces photograph shows the mushroom cloud rising above Nagasaki, Japan, on August 9, 1945, after the detonation of the 'Fat Man' plutonium atomic bomb — the second atomic bomb dropped by the United States. The first bomb, dropped on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945, killed approximately 80,000 people instantly. The Nagasaki bomb killed tens of thousands more. The atomic bombs were the product of the top-secret Manhattan Project, a massive scientific and industrial program involving more than 130,000 people and costing approximately $2 billion. President Truman authorized their use hoping to force Japan's surrender without a land invasion of Japan's home islands, which military planners projected would be extremely costly for both sides. Japan announced its surrender on August 15, 1945 (V-J Day), with the formal ceremony on September 2, 1945, ending World War II. The use of atomic bombs raised profound ethical questions that continue to be debated: Did the bombs save lives by ending the war quickly? Or were the bombings of predominantly civilian cities unjustifiable? The mushroom cloud remains one of the defining images of the twentieth century and of the nuclear age.

anchor.title: Yalta Conference, the Big Three: Churchill, Roosevelt, Stalin (February 1945)
anchor.creator: U.S. Army Signal Corps / U.S. Federal Government
anchor.citation: U.S. Army Signal Corps. "Yalta Conference, the Big Three: Churchill, Roosevelt, Stalin." Feb. 1945. National Archives and Records Administration, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Yalta_Conference_(Churchill,_Roosevelt,_Stalin)_(B%26W).jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white U.S. Army Signal Corps photograph showing the 'Big Three' Allied leaders — Prime Minister Winston Churchill, President Franklin D. Roosevelt, and Premier Joseph Stalin — seated together at Livadia Palace during the Yalta Conference, February 1945.
anchor.caption: This photograph from February 1945 shows the 'Big Three' Allied leaders — Prime Minister Winston Churchill of Great Britain (left), President Franklin D. Roosevelt of the United States (center), and Premier Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union (right) — seated together at the Yalta Conference, held at Livadia Palace in Crimea from February 4–11, 1945. The Yalta Conference was one of the most important diplomatic meetings of World War II. The three leaders agreed on plans to defeat Germany, divide it into occupation zones after the war, and establish the United Nations. They also agreed that Stalin would bring the Soviet Union into the war against Japan. However, agreements about free elections in Eastern Europe were soon violated by Stalin. This is one of the last photographs of President Roosevelt in good health; he died on April 12, 1945, just two months after Yalta. The tensions visible beneath the surface of Allied unity at Yalta soon developed into the Cold War between the democratic West and the communist East.

anchor.title: Signing of the Declaration by United Nations, Washington, D.C. (January 1, 1942)
anchor.creator: Unknown photographer / United Nations
anchor.citation: Unknown photographer. "Signing of the Declaration by United Nations, Washington, D.C." 1 Jan. 1942. United Nations, via Wikimedia Commons, commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Signing_Declaration_by_United_Nations.jpg.
anchor.alt: Black-and-white photograph showing representatives of 26 Allied nations, including President Franklin D. Roosevelt, signing the 'Declaration by United Nations' in Washington, D.C., January 1, 1942.
anchor.caption: This photograph shows the signing of the 'Declaration by United Nations' in Washington, D.C. on January 1, 1942 — the document that first officially used the name 'United Nations,' a term suggested by President Roosevelt. Representatives of 26 Allied nations pledged to support the Atlantic Charter and fight together against the Axis Powers without making separate peace agreements. This 1942 declaration was the seed from which the United Nations organization grew: it established the principle of collective Allied commitment and laid the diplomatic groundwork for the UN Charter signed in San Francisco on June 26, 1945. The United Nations was formally founded on October 24, 1945, just months after World War II ended, as world leaders were determined to create an international institution capable of preventing another world war. The United Nations Charter's preamble expressed the hope of saving 'succeeding generations from the scourge of war' — the direct lesson learned from two devastating world wars in thirty years.
